hints: Let $\mu$ be the population mean journey time now. $\text{H}_0$: it has not changed from the past value of 20.5 minutes. For $\text{H}_1$, the question asks whether the mean has **decreased**: which inequality is that, and is the test one-tailed or two-tailed?

If $\text{H}_0$ is true, the mean of a sample of 100 times is normal with mean 20.5 and standard deviation $\dfrac{1.2}{\sqrt{100}}$ (it is a mean of 100 values). Standardise: $z = \dfrac{20.3 - 20.5}{1.2/\sqrt{100}}$.
Work out the denominator first ($1.2$ divided by $\sqrt{100}$), then divide the top by it. Notice that 20.3 is below 20.5, so your $z$ should be negative.

This is a 4% one-tailed test in the lower tail: find the critical $z$ with $\Phi(z) = 0.96$ (use inverse normal) and put a minus sign on it. Compare your $z$ with it. Alternatively compare $\Phi(z)$ with $0.04$.

If your $z$ is beyond the critical value (further into the tail) you reject $\text{H}_0$; if not, you do not. Write the conclusion in the context of rail journey times, and not as a certainty ('there is evidence that...' or 'there is no evidence that...').
walkthrough:
**Define $\mu$ and set up the hypotheses (B1)**

Let $\mu$ be the **population mean** journey time (in minutes) since the new signals were installed. The old mean was $20.5$. We test whether the mean has **decreased**, so the alternative has a 'less than' sign, in a **one-tailed** test. Mark scheme: you must say 'population mean' (or use $\mu$), not just 'mean'.

$$\text{H}_0: \mu = 20.5$$

$$\text{H}_1: \mu < 20.5$$

**The distribution of the sample mean under $\text{H}_0$**

We assume $\text{H}_0$ is true. Single times have standard deviation $1.2$ (given unchanged). We test using the **mean of 100 times**, $\bar{X}$. A mean of 100 values varies less than one value, so its standard deviation is smaller:

$$\text{sd of } \bar{X} = \frac{1.2}{\sqrt{100}} = \frac{1.2}{10} = 0.12$$

Because $n = 100$ is large, $\bar{X}$ is approximately normal by the central limit theorem (so we do not need to know the shape of single journey times).

$$\bar{X} \sim \text{N}\left(20.5, 0.12^2\right) \text{ approximately}$$

**Standardise the sample mean (M1)**

The sample mean was $20.3$. Convert it to a $z$-value: sample mean minus the $\text{H}_0$ mean, divided by the standard deviation of the sample mean.

$$z = \frac{20.3 - 20.5}{1.2 \div \sqrt{100}} = \frac{-0.2}{0.12}$$

The M1 is for this expression. Common slip: dividing by $1.2$ and forgetting the $\sqrt{100}$.

**Calculate $z$ (A1)**

$$z = \frac{-0.2}{0.12} = -1.667$$

The negative sign tells us the sample mean is *below* the old mean, which is the direction $\text{H}_1$ expects. (If you compare areas instead, $\Phi(-1.667) = 0.0478$.)

**The critical value (second M1)**

The test is at the 4% level, one-tailed, with the whole 4% in the **lower** tail. The critical value $z_c$ satisfies $\Phi(z_c) = 0.04$. Equivalently, by symmetry, its magnitude satisfies $\Phi(z) = 0.96$. Use the calculator's inverse normal with area $0.96$, which gives $1.751$ (the scheme also accepts $1.75$). So the critical value is $-1.751$.

The rejection region is $z < -1.751$.

Compare: $-1.667$ is **not** below $-1.751$. Equivalently $1.667 < 1.751$.

Comparing areas gives the same decision: $0.0478 > 0.04$.

**Decision and conclusion in context (A1ft)**

Our $z = -1.667$ is not in the rejection region, so we **do not reject $\text{H}_0$**. The sample mean of 20.3 is lower than 20.5, but not low enough, at the 4% level, to be convincing: such a result could easily happen by chance if nothing had changed.

Conclusion in context, not definite: there is **no evidence** at the 4% level that the population mean journey time has decreased.

**Final answer**

$z = -1.667$, which is greater than the critical value $-1.751$ ($0.0478 > 0.04$), so $\text{H}_0$ is not rejected: there is no evidence that the (population) mean journey time has decreased.

hints: A Type II error means $\text{H}_0$ is **not rejected** although the true mean is 20.1. So first find the boundary of the rejection region for the sample mean, called the critical value $cv$: set $\dfrac{cv - 20.5}{1.2/\sqrt{100}}$ equal to the lower-tail critical $z$ from part (i).
Solve that equation for $cv$ (multiply by the denominator, then add 20.5). This is the sample mean below which the test rejects $\text{H}_0$.

Now suppose the true mean is $20.1$. Then the sample mean is normal with mean $20.1$ (and the same standard deviation $\dfrac{1.2}{\sqrt{100}}$). Standardise your $cv$: $z = \dfrac{cv - 20.1}{1.2/\sqrt{100}}$.
The test does **not** reject $\text{H}_0$ when the sample mean is **above** $cv$, so you need the upper-tail area: $\text{P}(Z > z) = 1 - \Phi(z)$.
Find $\Phi(z)$ with a normal table or the calculator's normal cdf, subtract from 1 and round to 3 s.f.
walkthrough:
**What a Type II error needs**

A **Type II error** is *not rejecting* $\text{H}_0$ when $\text{H}_0$ is actually false. Here, the true mean is now $20.1$ (not 20.5), so $\text{H}_0$ is false. We need the probability that the test still fails to reject $\text{H}_0$.

Two stages: (1) find which sample means *do* lead to rejecting $\text{H}_0$; (2) find the probability of **not** getting such a sample mean when the true mean is $20.1$.

**Find the critical value of the sample mean (M1*)**

Using the test from part (i), at the 4% level the critical $z$ is $-1.751$ (the value with $\Phi(z) = 0.04$). Under $\text{H}_0$ the sample mean has mean $20.5$ and standard deviation $\frac{1.2}{\sqrt{100}} = 0.12$. So the critical sample mean $cv$ satisfies

$$\frac{cv - 20.5}{1.2 \div \sqrt{100}} = -1.751$$

**Solve for $cv$ (A1)**

Multiply both sides by $0.12$:

$$cv - 20.5 = -1.751 \times 0.12 = -0.21012$$

Add 20.5:

$$cv = 20.5 - 0.21012 = 20.29\ldots$$

So $\text{H}_0$ is rejected when the sample mean is **below** about $20.29$ (the mark scheme accepts $20.3$). The A1 is for $20.29$ or $20.3$.

**Standardise using the true mean, 20.1 (DM1)**

Now suppose the true mean is $20.1$. The standard deviation of the sample mean is still $0.12$, but its centre is now $20.1$. The sample mean is no longer centred on $20.5$.

$$z = \frac{20.29 - 20.1}{1.2 \div \sqrt{100}} = \frac{0.19}{0.12} = 1.583$$

The scheme allows $20.3$ in place of $20.29$ here: $\frac{20.3 - 20.1}{0.12} = 1.667$.

**Choose the correct area (M1)**

The test does **not** reject $\text{H}_0$ when the sample mean is **above** $cv$. That is the area to the **right** of $z = 1.583$:

$$\text{P}(\text{Type II error}) = \text{P}(Z > 1.583) = 1 - \Phi(1.583)$$

Common slip: using $\Phi(1.583)$, the area to the *left*, which is the probability of *rejecting* $\text{H}_0$ (the power), not of a Type II error.

**Evaluate (A1)**

Normal table or calculator: $\Phi(1.583) = 0.9433$.

$$1 - 0.9433 = 0.0567$$

The mark scheme gives a range, $0.0567$ to $0.0569$, because of the rounding of $cv$. With the $20.3$ shortcut the answer is $1 - \Phi(1.667) = 0.0478$, which is also credited.

**Final answer**

$\text{P}(\text{Type II error}) = 0.0567$ (3 s.f.), anywhere in $0.0567$ to $0.0569$ is accepted.

hints: A Type II error means you do not reject $\text{H}_0$ when it is false. Say what $\text{H}_0$ claimed about the rail journey time, what is really true, and what the test wrongly concluded, in those terms.
walkthrough:
**What a Type II error is**

A Type II error is **not rejecting** $\text{H}_0$ when $\text{H}_1$ is actually true. Compare with Type I: rejecting $\text{H}_0$ when it is true.

**Put it into this context**

Here $\text{H}_0$ says the mean journey time has stayed the same, and $\text{H}_1$ says it has decreased. Not rejecting $\text{H}_0$ means concluding that the mean time has **not** decreased. The error is that this conclusion is wrong, because the mean time really **has** decreased. The mark scheme needs the answer in context.

**Final answer**

A Type II error is concluding that the (population) mean journey time has not decreased when, in fact, it has decreased.
